13 Minutes: A German carpenter comes within 13 minutes of killing Hitler with a bomb planted in a Munich beer hall in 1939. Based on the true story of Georg Elser, it is a taut thriller about one ordinary man who risked everything to change history — and why it failed.
1939 - Battle of Westerplatte: A Polish war film depicting the heroic defence of the Westerplatte garrison in Gdansk, where 182 Polish soldiers held out for seven days against vastly superior German forces at the opening of WWII. A monument to defiance against impossible odds.
1941: Steven Spielberg's satirical comedy depicting the mass panic that gripped Los Angeles after Pearl Harbor, as paranoid civilians and bumbling military scramble to defend against a feared Japanese invasion. More farce than history, but a unique take on the home front hysteria of December 1941.
1944: An Estonian war film following soldiers conscripted into both the German and Soviet armies — sometimes brothers fighting on opposite sides — during the brutal battles for Estonia in 1944. A rare look at a small nation crushed between two totalitarian powers.
A Bridge Too Far: Richard Attenborough's epic account of Operation Market Garden in September 1944 — the ambitious Allied plan to seize key Dutch bridges and outflank the German line. Despite stunning early successes, the operation collapsed at Arnhem, where British paratroopers were overrun waiting for armour that never arrived.
A French Village: A critically acclaimed French drama series following a small occupied village from the German invasion through liberation. Spanning seven seasons, it portrays collaboration, resistance, and moral compromise under Nazi occupation, showing how ordinary people make extraordinary choices.
A Hidden Life: Based on the true story of Austrian farmer Franz Jagerstatter, who refused to swear an oath to Hitler and serve in the Wehrmacht despite pressure from his village and the Church. Terrence Malick's meditative film follows his journey to execution in 1943, choosing conscience over survival.
A Midnight Clear: A group of exhausted American soldiers encounter a German unit willing to surrender in the Ardennes forest during the winter of 1944. An intimate anti-war film about the futility of killing among men who no longer believe in the cause they are fighting for.
A Small Light: A biographical drama about Miep Gies, the Dutch office worker who helped hide Anne Frank and her family in the Secret Annex in Amsterdam for over two years. It humanises those who risked their lives daily to protect the people they sheltered.
A Woman in Berlin: Based on an anonymous diary, this film portrays the mass rape of German women by Soviet soldiers during the fall of Berlin in April 1945. A devastating account of what happened to civilian women caught in the final battles of the war in Europe.
Adventures of a Mathematician: The story of Stanislaw Ulam, a Polish-Jewish mathematician who fled Europe for America and joined the Manhattan Project, helping design the hydrogen bomb. It explores the moral weight of scientific discovery and the immigrant experience in wartime America.
All the Light We Cannot See: Based on Anthony Doerr's Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, this Netflix series follows a blind French girl and a German radio operator whose lives intertwine in occupied Saint-Malo in 1944. A story of humanity amid the brutality of occupation and the war's final days.
Allied: A WWII thriller following a Canadian intelligence officer and a French Resistance fighter who fall in love during a dangerous mission in Casablanca. When they reunite in London, he is told she may be a German spy — and must discover the truth before it destroys them both.
Alone in Berlin: Based on Hans Fallada's novel, this film tells the true story of a German working-class couple who waged a silent campaign of resistance against the Nazi regime — leaving hundreds of postcards denouncing Hitler across Berlin — until the Gestapo tracked them down.
Anne Frank: The Whole Story: A comprehensive dramatisation of Anne Frank's life covering not only the years in hiding but her deportation to Auschwitz, transfer to Bergen-Belsen, and death just weeks before liberation. Based on Melissa Muller's biography, it gives full voice to Anne's story beyond the diary.
Anthropoid: Based on the true story of Operation Anthropoid — the Czech and Slovak paratroopers trained by the British who assassinated Reinhard Heydrich, one of the Holocaust's chief architects, in Prague in 1942. The assassination and its brutal aftermath are meticulously recreated.
April 9th: A Danish war film following a young officer whose bicycle infantry unit is thrown into the chaotic defence against Germany's surprise invasion of Denmark on April 9, 1940. It depicts the short, desperate, and ultimately futile resistance of a small nation caught unprepared.
Atonement: Joe Wright's acclaimed adaptation of Ian McEwan's novel, following how a young girl's false accusation destroys two lives across WWII — from the Dunkirk evacuation to the London Blitz. A story of guilt, war, and the stories we tell ourselves to survive.
Australia: Baz Luhrmann's sweeping epic set in Australia's Northern Territory during the Japanese threat following Pearl Harbor, following a British aristocrat and a cattle drover caught up in the war that reached Australia's shores.
Band of Brothers: Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks' landmark HBO miniseries follows Easy Company, 506th Regiment, 101st Airborne Division from training through D-Day, Market Garden, the Battle of the Bulge, and into Germany. Based on Stephen Ambrose's account of the real soldiers, it remains the definitive WWII television drama.
Battle for Sevastopol: A Ukrainian film telling the true story of Lyudmila Pavlichenko, the Soviet female sniper who became history's most successful with 309 confirmed kills. She fought in the brutal sieges of Odessa and Sevastopol before her story reached the world stage.
Before the Fall: Set in an elite Nazi boarding school in 1942, this German film follows a working-class boy who wins a scholarship to study among the sons of ideologues. A coming-of-age story showing how totalitarianism corrupts youth and erases individual identity.
Betrayed: A WWII drama following an American soldier who infiltrates a Dutch Nazi resistance network after being betrayed to the Germans, exploring the murky world of wartime intelligence and collaboration in occupied Netherlands.
Black Book: Paul Verhoeven's thriller follows Rachel Stein, a Dutch Jewish woman who joins the resistance after her family is murdered, going undercover as a cabaret singer to seduce a senior SS officer. A gripping story of survival where betrayal runs deep on both sides.
Black Rain: Shohei Imamura's devastating Japanese film follows a young woman whose chance of marriage is destroyed by radiation sickness after the Hiroshima bombing. Based on Masuji Ibuse's novel, it chronicles the lingering horror that continued long after August 1945.
Canopy: A minimalist Australian film following an ANZAC pilot shot down over Singapore jungle in 1942, who encounters a Chinese guerrilla fighter. With almost no dialogue, it explores survival and unexpected connection between two men who cannot speak each other's language.
Captain Corelli's Mandolin: Set on the Greek island of Kefalonia during Italian and German occupation, this romantic drama follows a young Greek woman's relationship with an Italian officer. Their idyll is destroyed when the Germans massacred the Italian garrison after Italy's 1943 armistice.
Catch-22: Joseph Heller's darkly comic novel brought to screen twice — as a 1970 film and a 2019 Hulu miniseries. Bombardier Yossarian tries to escape flying suicidal missions over Italy by claiming insanity, only to discover the circular logic of military bureaucracy makes escape impossible.
Churchill: Brian Cox portrays Winston Churchill in the tense days before D-Day, wrestling with doubt about Operation Overlord and fearing a repeat of the catastrophic Gallipoli landings. A character study of leadership under impossible pressure at the most consequential moment of the war.
City of Life and Death: Lu Chuan's stark black-and-white film depicting the Nanjing Massacre of 1937-38, when Japanese forces killed hundreds of thousands of Chinese civilians and prisoners of war. Shot with documentary realism, it remains one of cinema's most powerful accounts of WWII's greatest atrocities.
Colditz: A drama set in Colditz Castle, the supposedly escape-proof German prisoner of war camp where Allied officers deemed a security risk were imprisoned. It chronicles the ingenuity and camaraderie of British, French, Polish, and Dutch prisoners determined to escape at any cost.
Come and See: Elem Klimov's harrowing 1985 Soviet masterpiece follows a Belarusian boy who witnesses the systematic destruction of his village by German SS units. Widely considered the greatest anti-war film ever made — not for heroism, but for what war does to the human soul.
Conspiracy: A dramatisation of the 1942 Wannsee Conference, where fifteen senior Nazi officials coordinated the logistics of the Holocaust in 85 minutes. With Kenneth Branagh as Reinhard Heydrich, the film shows how genocide was reduced to bureaucratic procedure over lunch in a Berlin villa.
Countdown to War: A 1989 British drama depicting the final days of August 1939, as European leaders negotiated, bluffed, and ultimately failed to prevent the outbreak of war. A political thriller about how the world sleepwalked into the deadliest conflict in history.
Cross of Iron: Sam Peckinpah's brutal 1977 film follows a German sergeant on the Eastern Front who despises his officers' ideology more than he does the enemy. One of the few major WWII films told entirely from the German soldier's perspective, capturing the nihilistic horror of the Eastern Front.
Darkest Hour: Gary Oldman's Oscar-winning portrayal of Winston Churchill during the desperate weeks of May 1940, as Britain stood alone and the Prime Minister resisted pressure to negotiate with Hitler. The film's emotional peak comes as Churchill seeks the resolve of the British people.
Das Boot: Wolfgang Petersen's claustrophobic masterpiece follows the crew of a German U-boat on a brutal Atlantic patrol in 1941. Shot almost entirely inside the submarine, it captures the grinding monotony, terror, and mechanical failure that made submarine warfare the most psychologically punishing of any WWII theatre.
Death and Glory in Changde: A Chinese war epic depicting the Battle of Changde in 1943, where Nationalist Chinese forces held the city against a Japanese assault for weeks in one of the lesser-known but fiercely fought battles of the Second Sino-Japanese War.
Defiance: Edward Zwick's film tells the true story of the Bielski brothers, Belarusian Jews who escaped into the Naliboki Forest and built a community of over 1,200 Jewish refugees, evading German forces for years while the Holocaust raged around them.
Die Wannseekonferenz: A 2022 German dramatisation of the Wannsee Conference using the actual conference minutes as its script. It depicts the chilling banality with which Nazi officials coordinated mass murder, making it one of the most disturbing historical films about the Holocaust's administrative machinery.
Dieppe: A dramatisation of the disastrous Dieppe Raid of August 1942, where Allied forces — primarily Canadian — attempted an amphibious assault on the French port. Of 6,000 men landed, nearly 3,400 were killed, wounded, or captured in under nine hours.
Diplomacy: Volker Schlondorff's film depicts the tense negotiation on the night of August 24-25, 1944, when Swedish consul Raoul Nordling persuaded German General Dietrich von Choltitz not to carry out Hitler's order to destroy Paris before the Allied liberation.
Downfall: Bruno Ganz delivers a legendary performance as Adolf Hitler in his final days in the Berlin bunker in April 1945. Based on the memoirs of Hitler's secretary, the film humanises the monster to show how ordinary people enabled and served him until the very end — a landmark of German cinema.
Dunkirk: Christopher Nolan's technically stunning recreation of Operation Dynamo — the evacuation of over 330,000 Allied troops from the beaches of northern France in May-June 1940. Told simultaneously across land, sea, and air, it captures survival as an act of collective, desperate heroism.
El Alamein: The Line of Fire: An Italian war film following young soldiers through the North African campaign and the Second Battle of El Alamein in 1942. Shot on location in the Egyptian desert, it portrays the forgotten experience of Italian soldiers caught in Rommel's ultimately doomed desert war.
Emperor: A post-war drama following General Bonner Fellers as he investigates whether Emperor Hirohito should be tried as a war criminal after Japan's surrender. A political thriller exploring MacArthur's consequential decision to preserve the Emperor as a symbol of stability in occupied Japan.
Empire of the Sun: Steven Spielberg's adaptation of J.G. Ballard's semi-autobiographical novel follows a young British boy separated from his parents during the Japanese invasion of Shanghai in 1941. Interned in a Japanese POW camp, he navigates childhood amid the collapse of the colonial world he was born into.
En mai, fais ce qu'il te plait: A French drama depicting the chaotic mass exodus of civilians fleeing south during the German invasion of France in May-June 1940. Based on true events, it follows families caught in the largest internal migration in French history as their country collapsed in six weeks.
Enemy at the Gates: Jean-Jacques Annaud's thriller fictionalises the Battle of Stalingrad through a duel between Soviet sniper Vasily Zaitsev and a German expert marksman. While debated historically, it vividly captures the apocalyptic urban warfare that consumed the city across the winter of 1942-43.
Enola Gay: The Men, The Mission, The Ato: A 1980 American TV film dramatising the crew of the Enola Gay and the decision to drop the atomic bomb on Hiroshima. It examines the human side of the most consequential single military act of the twentieth century.
Escape from Sobibor: Based on the true story of the Sobibor extermination camp uprising in October 1943 — the most successful prisoner revolt in any Nazi death camp. Over 300 prisoners escaped; about 50 survived the war. A rare story of armed defiance from within the heart of the Holocaust.
Europa Europa: Agnieszka Holland's extraordinary film based on the true story of Solomon Perel, a German-Jewish boy who survived the Holocaust by hiding in plain sight — first in the Soviet Union, then being mistaken for an Aryan and enrolled in a Hitler Youth school after capture.
Fat Man and Little Boy: A dramatisation of the Manhattan Project focusing on the relationship between General Leslie Groves and J. Robert Oppenheimer as they raced to build the atomic bomb at Los Alamos. It explores the moral and political tensions that would reshape the post-war world.
Flags of Our Fathers: Clint Eastwood's film about the six men who raised the American flag on Iwo Jima and the propaganda machine that exploited the iconic photograph. Three survivors were brought home to sell war bonds, their real stories far more complicated than the image suggested.
Flame & Citron: A Danish thriller based on the true story of two resistance fighters — codenamed Flammen and Citronen — who carried out assassinations of Danish collaborators and German officers in occupied Copenhagen. One of the most decorated Danish films ever made.
Fury: David Ayer's gritty film follows a Sherman tank crew fighting through Germany in April 1945 as the war nears its end but the killing continues. Unflinching in its portrayal of combat fatigue, moral compromise, and the bonds forged between men who live and die together in a steel box.
Generation War: A German miniseries following five young Berlin friends who go their separate ways at the start of Operation Barbarossa — to the Eastern Front, to the resistance, to the stage — gradually losing everything they believed in. A sweeping, controversial portrait of ordinary Germans in extraordinary times.
Grave of the Fireflies: Isao Takahata's Studio Ghibli masterpiece follows two orphaned Japanese siblings struggling to survive after their mother dies in a firebombing raid near the war's end. One of the most devastating anti-war films ever made — all the more powerful for its animated form.
Greyhound: Tom Hanks as a US Navy commander on his first trans-Atlantic convoy command in 1942, hunted by a U-boat wolf pack across the Black Pit — the stretch of ocean beyond Allied air cover. Based on C.S. Forester's novel, it captures the relentless tension of the Battle of the Atlantic.
Hacksaw Ridge: Mel Gibson's film based on the true story of Desmond Doss, a conscientious objector who refused to carry a weapon yet won the Medal of Honor as a combat medic at Okinawa in 1945. He single-handedly saved 75 men by lowering them down an escarpment under fire.
Hamsun: A Norwegian drama about Nobel Prize-winning author Knut Hamsun, who collaborated with the Nazi occupiers of Norway and met Hitler in 1943. After the war he was put on trial and his reputation destroyed — a complex portrait of genius and catastrophic moral failure.
Hart's War: A legal thriller set in a German POW camp in 1944, where an African-American officer is accused of murder. A young American lieutenant takes on the defence, only to discover the trial is a cover for an escape attempt — forcing him to choose between truth and survival.
Hell in the Aegean: Based on the German assault on the Dodecanese islands in 1943 following Italy's armistice, depicting the chaotic Allied attempt to hold the islands and the swift German reconquest that followed Churchill's ill-fated Aegean strategy.
Hiroshima: A 1995 joint Canadian-Japanese production dramatising both the decision to drop the bomb in Washington and its aftermath in Hiroshima. It depicts the parallel perspectives of American military leaders and Japanese survivors at the same moment in history.
Hiroshima: Out of the Ashes: A 1990 American TV film depicting the aftermath of the atomic bombing from multiple perspectives — Japanese civilians, American prisoners of war, and a German Jesuit priest. One of the first productions to show the bomb's human consequences in unflinching detail.
Hitler: The Rise of Evil: A Canadian TV miniseries dramatising Hitler's rise from failed artist to dictator — from the Munich Beer Hall Putsch through his consolidation of power in 1934. Robert Carlyle portrays Hitler's psychological manipulation and charisma with chilling effectiveness.
Holocaust: A landmark 1978 American miniseries following two families — one Jewish, one a rising SS officer — across the entire Nazi period from 1935 to 1945. Enormously influential at the time, it introduced millions of viewers to the Holocaust and prompted West Germany's first national broadcast on the subject.
Hope and Glory: John Boorman's semi-autobiographical film about a young boy in bombed London during the Blitz, who finds the destruction magical — a playground of ruins and unexpected freedom. A unique perspective on the home front that captures childhood's capacity to find adventure in catastrophe.
Indigenes: A French-Algerian film following North African soldiers who fought under the French flag from Algeria to the liberation of Provence in 1944 — men who risked their lives for a France that refused to treat them as equals. The film led directly to the restoration of veterans' pensions denied to colonial troops.
Inglourious Basterds: Quentin Tarantino's alternate-history thriller set in occupied France, following a group of Jewish-American soldiers hunting Nazis and a Jewish cinema owner plotting her own revenge. Deliberately revisionist, it asks what cinema might do if it could rewrite history — and delivers a spectacularly violent answer.
Into the Storm: A 2009 HBO film depicting Winston Churchill during two defining moments: the darkest days of 1940 and the bittersweet victory of 1945, when the British public voted him out of office. Brendan Gleeson's portrayal completes the story begun in The Gathering Storm.
Into The White: Based on the true story of a British and German aircrew who both crash-land in the Norwegian mountains in 1940 and are forced to share a remote cabin to survive. As enemies become reluctant companions, the film explores the humanity beneath the uniform.
Jakob the Liar: Robin Williams in a rare dramatic role as a Jewish man in the Lodz Ghetto who claims to own a secret radio and uses fictional broadcasts of Allied victories to keep hope alive among his fellow prisoners. Based on Jurek Becker's novel, itself rooted in his childhood in the ghetto.
Jean Moulin: A French biographical drama about Jean Moulin, who became the most important figure in the French Resistance — unifying the fragmented movements under de Gaulle's authority before being captured by Gestapo chief Klaus Barbie in Lyon in 1943 and tortured to death.
John Rabe: The true story of John Rabe, a German Nazi Party member and Siemens director in Nanjing who established a safety zone during the 1937-38 Japanese massacre, sheltering over 200,000 Chinese civilians. His party membership provided protection — but became his downfall when he tried to tell the world.
Katyn: Andrzej Wajda's deeply personal film about the 1940 Katyn Forest massacre, in which the Soviet NKVD executed over 22,000 Polish officers and intellectuals. The son of one victim, Wajda waited forty years to make this monument to a crime the Soviets denied until 1990.
Kelly's Heroes: A 1970 caper film following American soldiers who go AWOL behind German lines in 1944 to steal 16 million dollars in Nazi gold. Part war film, part comedy, it satirises military hierarchy and the American obsession with profit even in wartime.
Land of Mine: A Danish film based on the true story of German prisoners of war forced to clear over two million land mines from Danish beaches after the war ended. Boys, mostly, sent to clear the deadly legacy of their own nation's occupation — many dying in the process.
Le Grand Charles: A French biographical drama tracing Charles de Gaulle's path from the fall of France through his years in London leading the Free French Forces to his triumphant return to Paris in 1944. A portrait of an outsized historical figure driven by an uncompromising vision of France.
Leningrad: A 2009 Russian-British film set during the 872-day Siege of Leningrad, following a British journalist trapped in the city as Soviet and German forces clash and civilians starve. Based on real accounts of the longest siege in modern warfare, in which over one million civilians died.
Letters from Iwo Jima: Clint Eastwood's companion piece to Flags of Our Fathers, told entirely from the Japanese perspective. Following General Kuribayashi and his men defending the volcanic island against the American assault in 1945, it humanises the enemy with remarkable empathy and dignity.
Life is Beautiful: Roberto Benigni's Oscar-winning film in which a Jewish-Italian man uses humour and imagination to shield his young son from the reality of a Nazi concentration camp. The first half is romantic comedy; the second a heartbreaking act of paternal love in the face of systematic murder.
Lore: An Australian-German film follows a teenage girl, the daughter of a senior SS officer, who leads her younger siblings across a destroyed Germany in 1945 after her parents' arrest. Her world view is shattered as she discovers the truth about what her parents' regime did.
Masters of the Air: The Apple TV+ continuation of the Spielberg-Hanks WWII series follows the 100th Bomb Group — the Bloody Hundredth — of the US Eighth Air Force flying catastrophically costly daylight bombing missions over occupied Europe. The air war companion to Band of Brothers and The Pacific.
Max Manus: The true story of Max Manus, Norway's most celebrated resistance fighter, who trained in Scotland and returned to sabotage German ships in Oslo harbour. A story of audacity, friendship, and the human cost of resistance, based on Manus's own memoir.
Memphis Belle: A dramatised account of the final mission of the Memphis Belle — one of the first B-17 bombers to complete 25 missions over Europe — and the crew who flew it. The film captures the tension and exhaustion of men who have survived against the odds and just want to go home.
Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence: David Bowie and Tom Conti in Nagisa Oshima's haunting film set in a Japanese POW camp in Java in 1942. An intense psychological power struggle between a British prisoner and a Japanese officer, exploring the clash between two cultures that cannot understand each other.
Midway: The original 1976 Midway film starring Charlton Heston, using dramatic recreation and authentic combat footage to depict the pivotal Pacific battle that ended Japanese naval dominance six months after Pearl Harbor.
Midway (2019): Roland Emmerich's blockbuster recreation of the Battle of Midway in June 1942, where the US Navy ambushed the Imperial Japanese fleet using broken codes and sank four aircraft carriers — turning the tide of the Pacific War in a single battle.
Miracle at St. Anna: Spike Lee's film about four African-American Buffalo Soldiers trapped in a Tuscan village in 1944. Based on James McBride's novel, it explores the experience of Black American soldiers fighting for a freedom denied to them at home.
Mission of the Shark: A dramatisation of the sinking of the USS Indianapolis, torpedoed in 1945 after delivering components for the atomic bomb. Its crew spent four days in shark-infested waters before rescue — one of the worst naval disasters in American history.
Munich: The Edge of War: Based on Robert Harris's novel, this Netflix thriller follows a British diplomat passing intelligence during the Munich Crisis of 1938, when Britain and France agreed to Hitler's annexation of the Sudetenland — a defining moment of appeasement that failed to prevent war.
Mussolini and I: An Italian miniseries depicting the final years of Mussolini's dictatorship, focusing on his son-in-law Count Galeazzo Ciano, who voted for Mussolini's removal in 1943 and was subsequently executed on the Duce's personal orders.
My Way: A Korean war film based on the extraordinary true story of Yang Kyoungjong, a Korean soldier who served successively in the Japanese, Soviet, and German armies — and was captured at Normandy wearing a German uniform in 1944.
Nacht und Nebel (Night and Fog): Alain Resnais' landmark 1956 documentary short intercutting contemporary footage of empty concentration camp grounds with archive footage of the camps in operation. One of the first films to confront the Holocaust directly, its final question — who is responsible? — remains unanswered.
Narvik: Hitler's First Defeat: A Norwegian film depicting the Battle of Narvik in April-May 1940, where Norwegian and Allied forces briefly recaptured the port from German forces — Hitler's first military setback. Told through the story of a Norwegian woman and her German-soldier husband on opposite sides.
Nuremberg: A 2000 Canadian TV film starring Alec Baldwin as chief prosecutor Robert Jackson at the Nuremberg Trials of 1945-46. It depicts the landmark proceedings that established crimes against humanity as an international legal concept and held the Nazi leadership accountable.
Operation Finale: The true story of the 1960 Mossad operation to capture Adolf Eichmann — the SS officer who coordinated the logistics of the Holocaust — hiding in Buenos Aires under a false identity. A thriller about justice, memory, and the long reach of history.
Operation Mincemeat: Colin Firth in the true story of Operation Mincemeat — the British intelligence deception in which a corpse carrying false documents was planted off the coast of Spain to mislead the Germans about the 1943 Allied invasion target, helping ensure the success of the Sicily landings.
Oppenheimer: Christopher Nolan's epic biography of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the physicist who led the Manhattan Project and oversaw the first atomic bomb test at Trinity. The film spans his career, the bomb, and his post-war security hearing — a meditation on genius, politics, and moral consequence.
Overlord: Stuart Cooper's 1975 British film blending fictional narrative with authentic wartime newsreel footage, following a young recruit from training through the Normandy landings. A unique aesthetic experiment that captures the anonymous, industrial nature of total war.
Panfilov's 28 Men: A Russian war film depicting the legendary last stand of 28 soldiers who allegedly stopped a German tank assault near Moscow in November 1941 — none surviving. Whatever the historical truth, the story became one of the defining myths of Soviet resistance.
Paradise Road: Based on the true experiences of Allied women prisoners held in Japanese camps in Sumatra, who formed a vocal orchestra — singing transcriptions of classical pieces — as an act of defiance and spiritual sustenance. Glenn Close leads the story of women's courage under captivity.
Patton: George C. Scott's Oscar-winning portrayal of General George S. Patton — the brilliant, bombastic American commander who drove from North Africa through the liberation of Europe. One of cinema's great character studies of a man simultaneously larger than life and dangerously out of control.
Pearl Harbor: Michael Bay's blockbuster dramatisation of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, framed around a love triangle between two American pilots and a nurse. It vividly recreates the attack that brought America into WWII.
Race: The story of Jesse Owens at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, where the Black American athlete won four gold medals under Hitler's gaze, directly refuting Nazi theories of Aryan supremacy. A film about speed, dignity, and the weaponisation of sport.
Red Tails: George Lucas' film about the Tuskegee Airmen — the African-American pilots of the 332nd Fighter Group who proved their worth over Italy and became legendary for never losing a bomber under their escort. A story of excellence defeating prejudice in the skies over Europe.
Resistance (2020): Jesse Eisenberg as Marcel Marceau — the famous mime — who as a young Jewish man in occupied France helped smuggle hundreds of Jewish children to safety in Switzerland. A little-known true story about one of the twentieth century's most recognisable artists.
Saints and Soldiers: A low-budget American film about American soldiers separated from their unit during the Malmedy Massacre in December 1944, making their way back to Allied lines through the Belgian Ardennes with vital intelligence about German positions.
Sands of Iwo Jima: John Wayne's 1949 film following a Marine sergeant who drills his men hard before the assault on Iwo Jima. The film recreated the flag-raising on Mount Suribachi using the actual men from the famous photograph, three of whom appear in the film.
SAS: Rogue Heroes: A BBC dramatisation based on Ben Macintyre's book about the founding of the SAS in the North African desert in 1941 by David Stirling, who convinced a sceptical Army establishment to let him try deep-penetration raids on German airfields. Audacious, irreverent, and surprisingly funny.
Saving Private Ryan: Steven Spielberg's landmark film opens with the most visceral recreation of combat ever filmed — the D-Day landings at Omaha Beach — before following Captain Miller's squad across Normandy on a mission to find the last surviving son of a family that has lost three boys to the war.
Schindler's List: Steven Spielberg's masterpiece — shot in black and white in Krakow — tells the true story of Oskar Schindler, a German businessman who used his factory to save over 1,100 Jewish workers from the death camps. The most important Holocaust film ever made.
Snow Falling on Cedars: Set on a Pacific Northwest island in 1951, this mystery revisits wartime injustice as a Japanese-American fisherman is tried for murder. Told in flashback, it explores the internment of Japanese-Americans and the wounds left by war on a small coastal community.
Soldier of Orange: Paul Verhoeven's autobiographical film follows a group of Dutch students whose lives diverge dramatically after the German invasion — some joining the resistance, some collaborating. Rutger Hauer stars in this landmark of Dutch cinema based on the true memoir of Erik Hazelhoff Roelfzema.
Son of Saul: Laszlo Nemes' Hungarian film, shot in extreme close-up, follows Saul Auslaender, a Sonderkommando at Auschwitz-Birkenau forced to assist in the genocide he is part of. When he finds a body he believes is his son's, he embarks on a desperate mission to give the boy a proper burial.
Sophie Scholl: The Final Days: Based on Gestapo interrogation transcripts, this German film depicts the last six days of Sophie Scholl — the 21-year-old who distributed anti-Nazi leaflets with the White Rose resistance group and was arrested, tried, and guillotined in February 1943.
Stalingrad: A 2013 Russian blockbuster depicting the Battle of Stalingrad from the Soviet perspective, following soldiers defending a ruined building and the civilians they protect. Made in 3D on the 70th anniversary of the German surrender.
Stalingrad (1993): A German film following Wehrmacht soldiers through the catastrophic Stalingrad campaign of 1942-43 — from their arrival in the city to the destruction of the Sixth Army. One of the most honest German films about the Eastern Front, told entirely from the losers' perspective.
Suite Francaise: Based on Irene Nemirovsky's unfinished novel — discovered in her daughter's attic sixty years after its author died at Auschwitz — depicting a French town under German occupation in 1940-41, and the forbidden love between a Frenchwoman and a German officer billeted in her home.
Sunshine: Istvan Szabo's Hungarian epic follows three generations of a Jewish-Hungarian family who change their name to assimilate, serve successive regimes, and lose something of themselves with each accommodation. A century of Central European Jewish history compressed into one family's tragedy.
Talvisota: The definitive Finnish film about the Winter War — the Soviet invasion of Finland in 1939-40 — following Finnish reservists defending their homeland against overwhelming Soviet forces. Finland's extraordinary resistance, killing four Soviet soldiers for every Finn lost, is chronicled with grim realism.
The 12th Man: A Norwegian film based on the true story of Jan Baalsrud, a commando who escaped a German ambush in 1943 and survived two months in the Arctic — frostbitten, snowblind, hunted — before reaching neutral Sweden with the help of Norwegian civilians who risked everything to save him.
The Auschwitz Report: A Czech-Slovak film based on the true story of two Slovakian prisoners who escaped Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1944 and compiled a detailed report documenting the mass murder — the Vrba-Wetzler Report, eventually delivered to the Allies and the Vatican.
The Battle of Britain: A 1969 British epic depicting the RAF's defence against the Luftwaffe during the summer of 1940 — the aerial campaign that forced Hitler to postpone his invasion. Featuring actual Spitfires and Hurricanes, it remains the most accurate recreation of air combat in cinema history.
The Battle of Neretva: A 1969 Yugoslav epic following Tito's Partisans as they break through a combined German, Italian, Chetnik, and Ustasha encirclement in Bosnia in 1943. One of the most ambitious European war films ever made.
The Big Red One: Sam Fuller's autobiographical film follows a squad of the 1st Infantry Division from North Africa through Sicily, Normandy, Belgium, and the liberation of a concentration camp. Based on Fuller's own wartime experiences, it captures both the camaraderie and senselessness of combat.
The Book Thief: Based on Markus Zusak's novel narrated by Death, this film follows a young German girl living near Munich who steals books and hides a Jewish man in the basement during the war. A story about the power of words in a world trying to destroy them.
The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas: Based on John Boyne's novel, this film depicts a friendship between Bruno, the eight-year-old son of an Auschwitz commandant, and Shmuel, a Jewish boy on the other side of the fence. Used globally as an educational tool about the Holocaust.
The Brest Fortress: A Belarusian film depicting the defence of the Brest Fortress in June 1941, where Soviet soldiers held out against the initial German Blitzkrieg for nearly a month despite being completely surrounded — one of the opening battles of Operation Barbarossa.
The Bridge at Remagen: A 1969 American film depicting the capture of the Ludendorff Bridge at Remagen in March 1945 — the last intact bridge across the Rhine and an unexpected opportunity that allowed Allied forces to pour into Germany weeks ahead of schedule.
The Bridge on the River Kwai: David Lean's Oscar-winning classic follows British prisoners of war building a railway bridge for the Japanese in Burma. The tension between Colonel Nicholson — who insists his men build the bridge with military pride — and the Allied commando sent to destroy it makes this one of cinema's most morally complex war films.
The Captain: Based on the true story of Willi Herold, a German deserter who found an abandoned captain's uniform in 1945 and used it to impersonate an officer — executing prisoners and commandeering a POW camp. A darkly comic film about authority, obedience, and the collapse of a murderous state.
The Champion of Auschwitz: A Polish film depicting the true story of Tadeusz Pietrzykowski, a boxer who survived Auschwitz by fighting for the entertainment of SS guards, winning over 40 fights against opponents much larger than himself. Sport as a means of survival.
The Children of Huang Shi: Based on the true story of British journalist George Hogg, who during the Second Sino-Japanese War took charge of an orphanage and led sixty orphaned children on a 700-mile trek across the Gobi Desert to safety.
The Conference: A 2022 German film reimagining the Wannsee Conference, focusing on the bureaucratic and ideological dynamics among the Nazi officials who coordinated the Final Solution. Part of a wave of recent German productions confronting the Holocaust's administrative machinery.
The Counterfeiters: Stefan Ruzowitzky's Oscar-winning Austrian film based on Operation Bernhard — the Nazi scheme to counterfeit British and American currency using Jewish prisoners at Sachsenhausen. The moral dilemma: participate and survive, or sabotage the operation and likely die.
The Desert Fox: A 1951 film portraying Field Marshal Erwin Rommel as a brilliant soldier of honour who turned against Hitler after Normandy and was implicated in the July 1944 plot. James Mason's Rommel became the template for the contested myth of the honourable German officer.
The Dirty Dozen: A 1967 action classic in which a maverick Army major trains twelve convicted criminals for a suicidal mission behind German lines. A counterculture classic that questioned military authority and the morality of using violence to fight violence — and an enduring template for the commando genre.
The Eight Hundred: Zhang Yimou's spectacular film depicting the 524th Regiment's defence of the Sihang Warehouse in Shanghai in October 1937, fighting across from the International Settlement whose residents watched from the opposite bank. The most expensive Chinese film ever made.
The English Patient: Anthony Minghella's Oscar-winning epic follows a badly burned Hungarian cartographer through the final months of the war in Italy, as his tragic wartime love affair in North Africa is slowly revealed. Based on Michael Ondaatje's Booker Prize-winning novel.
The Exception: A thriller set in occupied Netherlands in 1940, where a German soldier sent to protect the exiled Kaiser Wilhelm II falls for a Dutch housemaid who may be a British spy. An exploration of loyalty, complicity, and desire under occupation.
The Flowers of War: Zhang Yimou's film depicting the Nanjing Massacre through the eyes of an American mortician sheltering Chinese schoolgirls and bar girls in a cathedral. Christian Bale leads a production that brought one of WWII's worst atrocities to international audiences.
The Forgotten Battle: A Dutch Netflix film set during the Allied assault on the Scheldt estuary in Zeeland in 1944, following Dutch collaborators, resistance fighters, a British airborne soldier, and a German tank operator whose lives intersect during the deadly battle to open the port of Antwerp.
The Gathering Storm: A BBC film depicting Churchill in the political wilderness of the 1930s — warning about Hitler while being dismissed by the British establishment. Albert Finney's quiet, defiant Churchill shows the years of frustration before his return to power in 1939.
The Good German: Steven Soderbergh's noir thriller set in post-war Berlin in 1945, shot in black-and-white in the style of a 1940s Hollywood film. An American journalist becomes entangled in a murder mystery leading back to a wartime atrocity and the woman he once loved.
The Great Escape: John Sturges' classic 1963 adventure based on the true mass escape from Stalag Luft III in March 1944, in which 76 Allied prisoners broke out through hand-dug tunnels. Only three made it to freedom; 50 were executed on Hitler's personal orders. Steve McQueen leads the all-star cast.
The Great Raid: Based on the Cabanatuan Raid of January 1945, in which US Rangers and Filipino guerrillas rescued over 500 American prisoners from a Japanese camp — one of the most successful rescue missions in military history, accomplished with remarkable speed and minimal casualties.
The Grey Zone: Tim Blake Nelson's devastating film set in Auschwitz-Birkenau, following Sonderkommando — Jewish prisoners forced to work in the crematoria — who planned the only armed uprising in the camp in October 1944. A brutal examination of impossible moral choices.
The Guns of Navarone: A 1961 adventure classic following an Allied commando team sent to destroy two massive German guns on a Greek island blocking a naval operation. A template for the behind-enemy-lines genre that spawned countless imitators.
The Heroes of Telemark: A 1965 British war film based on Operation Gunnerside — the Norwegian resistance mission to destroy the heavy water plant at Vemork in 1943, denying the Germans a key component for a potential atomic weapon. Kirk Douglas leads the saboteurs through the Norwegian winter.
The Imitation Game: The story of Alan Turing — the Cambridge mathematician who led the team that broke the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park, arguably shortening the war by years — and his subsequent persecution for being gay. Benedict Cumberbatch brought Turing's story to global audiences.
The King's Choice: A Norwegian film depicting King Haakon VII's refusal to surrender to Germany in April 1940, forcing the government into exile rather than collaborate. A study in royal leadership and moral courage, showing one man's decision that shaped an occupied nation's identity for decades.
The King's Speech: The story of King George VI's struggle to overcome his stammer with the help of an unconventional Australian speech therapist, culminating in his address to the British people on the declaration of war in 1939. Colin Firth won an Oscar as the reluctant king.
The Last Frontier: A Russian war film depicting the defence of Moscow in the winter of 1941-42, when Soviet forces held the German advance at the city's gates — the first major German defeat on the Eastern Front and the end of the myth of Blitzkrieg invincibility.
The Longest Day: Darryl F. Zanuck's 1962 epic depicting the D-Day landings from multiple perspectives — American, British, French, and German. With an all-star cast and filmed on the actual Normandy beaches, it remains the most comprehensive cinematic account of Operation Overlord ever made.
The Man Who Will Come: An Italian film depicting the Marzabotto massacre of September-October 1944, in which SS troops killed over 770 Italian civilians in the Apennines in reprisal for partisan activity. One of the worst atrocities committed in Western Europe during the war.
The Man with the Iron Heart: Based on Laurent Binet's novel, this film depicts Operation Anthropoid — the assassination of Reinhard Heydrich in Prague in 1942 — intercut with the rise of Heydrich himself. Jason Clarke portrays one of the Holocaust's most feared architects.
The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare: Guy Ritchie's action-comedy based on the true story of the Special Operations Executive and their most daring missions, including the 1942 raid on Spanish Guinea that stole German and Italian vessels from neutral harbours. Based on Ben Macintyre's book.
The Monuments Men: Based on the true story of the Monuments, Fine Arts and Archives unit — Allied soldiers tasked with protecting Europe's cultural heritage from Nazi looting. George Clooney leads an ensemble cast hunting stolen art before the Red Army could claim it.
The Narrow Road to the Deep North: An Australian adaptation of Richard Flanagan's Booker Prize-winning novel following an Australian POW surgeon on the Burma-Thailand Railway and the decades-long trauma that follows him home. A meditation on survival, guilt, and what we owe the dead.
The Pacific: Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks' companion series to Band of Brothers follows three Marines — Robert Leckie, John Basilone, and Eugene Sledge — through the island-hopping campaign against Japan. From Guadalcanal to Okinawa, it captures a theatre defined by brutality, disease, and racial hatred.
The People vs Fritz Bauer: A German legal thriller about Frankfurt Attorney General Fritz Bauer, who in 1958 secretly tipped off the Mossad about Eichmann's location in Argentina — because he didn't trust his own colleagues, many former Nazis, to prosecute him in German courts.
The Pianist: Roman Polanski's autobiographical film based on the memoirs of Wladyslaw Szpilman, a Polish-Jewish pianist who survived the destruction of the Warsaw Ghetto by hiding in bombed ruins — sustained by music and the unexpected help of a German officer who found him at an abandoned piano. Adrien Brody won the Oscar.
The Plot Against America: Philip Roth's alternate history — in which Charles Lindbergh defeats FDR in 1940 and steers America toward isolationism — adapted as an HBO miniseries. A story about a Jewish family in New Jersey whose ordinary life is slowly poisoned by fascism creeping into their country.
The Railway Man: The true story of Eric Lomax, a British POW tortured by the Japanese on the Burma-Thailand Railway who spent forty years consumed by trauma and hatred — until an unexpected reunion with his torturer led to forgiveness. Colin Firth and Jeremy Irvine play Lomax at different ages.
The Reader: Kate Winslet's Oscar-winning role as Hanna Schmitz, a German woman who has an affair with a teenage boy in post-war Germany — only for him to encounter her years later as a defendant at a war crimes trial for her actions as an Auschwitz guard. A film about complicity and the burden of the Nazi generation.
The Resistance Banker: A Dutch film based on the true story of Walraven van Hall, a bank director who secretly embezzled millions from his own bank to fund the Dutch resistance — paying for false documents, hiding Jews, supporting strikes — until his arrest and execution in March 1945.
The Scarlet and the Black: Gregory Peck as Monsignor Hugh O'Flaherty, the Vatican priest who hid thousands of Allied POWs, Jews, and partisans under the noses of the Nazis in Rome. Based on the true story of the Vatican escape line that defied the Gestapo's most determined attempts to shut it down.
The Shadow in My Eye: A Danish film depicting the Copenhagen School bombing of March 1945, when the Royal Air Force accidentally bombed a French school near a Gestapo headquarters, killing 86 Danish children and 18 adults. A rare examination of Allied mistakes and civilian casualties.
The Tattooist of Auschwitz: Based on Heather Morris's bestselling novel about Lale Sokolov, a Slovakian Jewish prisoner who tattooed numbers onto his fellow inmates at Auschwitz and fell in love with one of them. A love story that sustained two people through three years of the Holocaust.
The Thin Red Line: Terrence Malick's philosophical war film follows a US Army company during the Battle of Guadalcanal. Unlike traditional combat films, it meditates on nature, beauty, and violence — an interior war film told through competing voices searching for meaning in the madness of the Pacific.
The Tuskegee Airmen: A 1995 HBO film about the first African-American military aviators — the men who trained at Tuskegee, Alabama and became the 332nd Fighter Group. Starring Laurence Fishburne, it brought the story of these pioneering pilots to mainstream audiences before Red Tails.
The Warrior's Heart: A drama following a young American soldier whose WWII service shapes his understanding of duty, sacrifice, and what it means to serve. A character-driven exploration of the impact of war on identity and the bonds formed under combat.
The Way Back: Peter Weir's survival film based on the disputed memoir of Slawomir Rawicz, depicting the escape of Polish prisoners from a Siberian gulag in 1941 and their 4,000-mile trek through Mongolia, the Gobi Desert, and the Himalayas to British India.
The Windermere Children: A BBC film depicting the true story of 300 young Holocaust survivors brought to the Lake District in 1945 to begin recovery. One of the few WWII films focused entirely on healing rather than fighting, it shows the enormous task of rebuilding lives shattered by the camps.
The Zookeeper's Wife: Based on the true story of Jan and Antonina Zabinski, who used Warsaw Zoo's bombed-out enclosures to hide over 300 Jews from the Ghetto. Jessica Chastain plays Antonina, who harboured refugees under the nose of the German commandant who took over the zoo.
They Fought for Their Motherland: A 1975 Soviet epic based on Mikhail Sholokhov's unfinished novel, following a battered Red Army regiment defending a Don River crossing during the German summer offensive of 1942. A tribute to ordinary Soviet soldiers in the tradition of socialist realism.
Thirty Seconds Over Tokyo: A 1944 American film based on the true story of the Doolittle Raid — the audacious B-25 bombing mission of April 1942 that struck Tokyo just four months after Pearl Harbor, demonstrating Japan was not invulnerable and providing a crucial morale boost to the American public.
To End All Wars: Based on Ernest Gordon's memoir, this film follows British POWs on the Burma-Thailand Railway who find spiritual strength in forming a secret university and performing plays, while others collaborate with their guards. A study in how different men respond to imprisonment and suffering.
Tobruk: A 1967 American war film about a mission to blow up Rommel's fuel depot at Tobruk before the El Alamein offensive — using German-Jewish soldiers from Palestine disguised as prisoners escorted by British Commandos through the Libyan desert.
Tora! Tora! Tora!: A joint American-Japanese production depicting the attack on Pearl Harbor from both perspectives simultaneously. Released in 1970, it remains the most historically accurate account of the attack — showing the meticulous Japanese planning and the American intelligence failures that allowed it to succeed.
Unbroken: Based on Laura Hillenbrand's biography of Louis Zamperini — Olympic runner, B-24 bombardier, and crash survivor who spent 47 days on a life raft before Japanese capture and years of brutal imprisonment. Directed by Angelina Jolie, it is a story of extraordinary human endurance.
Uprising: A 2001 TV film depicting the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of April-May 1943, in which Jewish fighters armed with improvised weapons held off the SS for four weeks — the longest urban resistance of WWII. Hank Azaria, David Schwimmer, and Jon Voight lead the cast.
USS Indianapolis: Men of Courage: Nicolas Cage in a dramatisation of the sinking of the USS Indianapolis in July 1945 and the four-day ordeal of survivors in shark-infested waters before accidental rescue. The Navy's deadliest single-ship loss — and the incident behind Quint's famous monologue in Jaws.
Valkyrie: Tom Cruise as Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg, the German officer who planted a briefcase bomb under the conference table in Hitler's Wolf's Lair headquarters on July 20, 1944. The conspiracy involved hundreds of senior officials and came within minutes of succeeding.
Walking with the Enemy: Based on the true story of Pinchas Rosenbaum, a young Hungarian Jew who disguised himself in an Arrow Cross uniform to save fellow Jews from deportation during the final German occupation of Hungary in 1944.
War Sailor: A Norwegian miniseries based on the true stories of Norwegian merchant sailors who served on Allied convoys throughout WWII — the most dangerous occupation of any Norwegian in the war — and their impossibly difficult return to civilian life when it ended.
We Were the Lucky Ones: Based on Georgia Hunter's novel tracing her own family's story, following a Polish Jewish family separated at the start of WWII who find extraordinary ways to survive on five continents, guided by the desperate hope of reuniting after the war.
When Trumpets Fade: A 1998 HBO film about a sole survivor of a battle in the Hurtgen Forest who is promoted against his will and forced back into combat. A bleak study of a man for whom survival instinct directly conflicts with military duty — and heroism means something entirely different.
Where Eagles Dare: Richard Burton and Clint Eastwood in a 1968 action classic in which Allied commandos storm an impregnable Alpine castle to rescue an American general — only for nothing to be quite as it seems. Pure entertainment, spectacularly executed, and one of the great WWII adventure films.
Windtalkers: John Woo's film about a Marine assigned to protect a Navajo Code Talker on Saipan — with secret orders to kill him if capture is imminent. The Navajo code, based on an unwritten language, was never broken by Japan and played a crucial role in Pacific communications.
Winter in Wartime: A Dutch film set in occupied Netherlands in 1945, following a 14-year-old boy who helps a wounded British airman escape from German occupation — and discovers that resistance and collaboration are more complicated than he imagined, even within his own family.
World on Fire: A BBC drama following characters across Britain, Germany, France, and Poland in the first years of the war, exploring how the conflict reshapes ordinary lives on both sides of the front. A human-scale portrait of WWII's early years through interconnected stories.
